liturgical_day: Wednesday of the Eighteenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: A foreign woman will not stop shouting until the mercy she knows is real has arrived.
reflection:
Today the liturgy sets two kinds of persistence side by side. In the first reading, God persists in love for a people who have been scattered and broken. In the Gospel, a woman persists in love for her daughter, pressing through every obstacle until Jesus answers her. Neither the love of God nor the love of this mother can be finally deflected, and that is worth sitting with over your first cup of coffee.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 31:1-7**

Chapter 31 of Jeremiah is one of the most luminous passages in the entire Hebrew Bible, and it arrives late in a book that has been extraordinarily dark. The prophet Jeremiah spent his life delivering unwelcome news to a nation careening toward catastrophe, and for most of the book, the catastrophe duly arrives: siege, defeat, exile, the burning of Jerusalem, the end of everything the people thought was guaranteed. Chapters 30 through 33 are sometimes called "the Book of Consolation," a sudden turn in a book of lament, and today's passage is near its beginning.

What God is promising here is restoration to a people already in exile — people who have lost the land, the temple, the king, and their working assumptions about how the world works. The images God reaches for are not institutional or political. They are domestic, bodily, festive. Tambourines. Dancing. The planting of vineyards and actually getting to eat the fruit — which sounds simple until you recall that throughout the invasion and deportation, others had been eating their fruit. The watchmen calling from Mount Ephraim — Ephraim is the northern kingdom, long gone and seemingly beyond recovery — saying "Rise up, let us go to Zion." Even the lost tribes are folded back in.

The phrase that anchors all of this is striking in its plainness: "With age-old love I have loved you." The Hebrew underneath suggests something like a love that precedes everything, that existed before the nation's history began. This is not reward for faithfulness — the people have not been faithful — but something closer to a love that simply is, the way the sun simply is, and that cannot be permanently blocked. The psalm today is drawn from the same chapter of Jeremiah, continuing the same movement: he who scattered now gathers, mourning turns to joy, even the old and the young dance together. The psalm answers the reading not as commentary but as echo, the way a valley returns a shout.

**The Gospel — Matthew 15:21-28**

This is one of the more uncomfortable passages in the Gospels, and it is a sign of the text's honesty that it was preserved. Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon — Gentile territory, well outside Israel. A Canaanite woman comes shouting after him. The label "Canaanite" is deliberately archaic; Matthew is using the old name, not the Roman-era name "Syrophoenician" that Mark uses. It reaches back centuries and calls to mind everything in Israelite history that separated these peoples. She is not just a foreigner; she is the foreigner.

She calls him "Lord, Son of David," which is a Jewish messianic title — she knows exactly who she is addressing. He says nothing. The disciples want her gone. He tells her his mission is to Israel. She kneels and says simply, "Lord, help me." Then comes the hard line: it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs. The word for dogs here is the diminutive, meaning household dogs rather than strays, but it is still a sharp thing to say, and the tradition has never quite agreed on what to make of it. What is not in dispute is what happens next: she takes the image and runs with it. Even the dogs eat the scraps from the table. She does not argue the premise; she finds the mercy hiding inside the metaphor and pulls it out.

Jesus's response is immediate and unconditional. "O woman, great is your faith." He does not say great is your argument, though her argument was sharp. Faith, in Matthew's vocabulary, is not primarily an intellectual position — it is a posture of complete reliance, a refusal to give up on the one you believe can help. Her daughter is healed at that moment, from a distance, the way all healing that comes from God comes: across whatever gap seemed uncrossable.

**Faith that will not take silence for an answer**

What Jeremiah's exiles and this woman share is a refusal to accept the apparent finality of their situation. The exiles have every worldly reason to believe it is over — the city is ash, the king is gone, the land belongs to someone else. The woman has every social reason to accept the rebuff — she is outside the chosen people, outside the mission, told as plainly as possible that this is not for her. Both press forward anyway, and in both cases the pressing forward is met by a love that was apparently already looking for the occasion to show itself.

There is something quietly radical in the way the Gospel handles this. The mercy of God, which Jeremiah says is age-old, is not a reward dispensed to insiders. It is something a foreign woman who refuses to quit can reach out and take hold of. The children's bread, as it turns out, is abundant enough to drop crumbs, and those crumbs are themselves miraculous.

**To carry today**

Think of the thing you have quietly filed away as settled — the door that seems closed, the situation you have stopped praying about because it feels finished. The woman in today's Gospel did not accept silence as a final answer, and Jesus honored that. Bring it back to prayer today, not as a demand but as the honest claim of someone who has not stopped believing that mercy is real.

liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint John Vianney, Priest
epigraph: God names the wound honestly, then promises to heal it anyway.
reflection:
There is a particular kind of honesty that only someone who loves you can deliver — the kind that names how bad things really are before offering any comfort. The Book of Jeremiah is full of this, and today's passage is one of its most striking examples. God speaks with a directness that could sound brutal, and then, without pausing for breath, turns entirely toward restoration. This is the shape of the day: wound named, then healed; sinking acknowledged, then caught.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 30:1-2, 12-15, 18-22**

We are deep in what scholars sometimes call the "Book of Consolation," chapters 30 and 31 of Jeremiah, which sit like an island of hope inside one of the bleakest prophetic books in the Bible. Jeremiah has spent most of his ministry delivering terrible news to Judah — conquest is coming, the city will fall, there is no avoiding it. And then he is told to write something down. The instruction to *write* is itself significant; this is a word meant to outlast the moment, a promise intended for future generations to read.

What gets written begins with frank diagnosis. The wound is "incurable," the bruise "grievous." No one is coming to advocate for Israel's case. The "lovers" who have abandoned the people are the foreign powers Judah courted for security — Egypt, Assyria — political alliances made instead of trusting God. They have vanished, as fair-weather allies do. God says plainly: this suffering came from real guilt, not from accident or bad luck. There is something almost merciful in this refusal to soften the picture. A physician who tells you exactly what is wrong, even when it is serious, is treating you as someone who can bear the truth.

Then the turn. "See! I will restore the tents of Jacob." The word "tents" reaches back to the wilderness wandering, to the portable, provisional life before Israel had cities and palaces — God is remembering the whole story of his people, not just the recent disaster. The city will be rebuilt. Songs will come back. The population will grow again. And then the most intimate promise in the passage: "When I summon him, he shall approach me" — which the text itself glosses as an almost impossible intimacy, one that ordinarily carries a mortal risk. The people will be near enough to come when called. The covenant formula that closes the reading — "You shall be my people, and I will be your God" — is one of the oldest refrains in all of Scripture, and hearing it after all that darkness carries enormous weight.

Psalm 102 follows naturally, almost as Israel's response to what God has just promised. It is the psalm of someone who has been in ruins — the psalmist speaks from exactly the condition Jeremiah described — and who lifts their eyes toward a God who "regarded the prayer of the destitute, and not despised their prayer." The refrain, "The Lord will build up Zion again, and appear in all his glory," is not wishful thinking; it is confidence built on what God has done before.

**The Gospel — Matthew 14:22-36**

The walking on the water is one of those stories that has been so often illustrated and summarized that we can forget how strange and particular it is. Jesus has just fed the five thousand, a moment of enormous public energy, and he sends everyone away — the crowds and then even the disciples — so that he can go up the mountain to pray. He is alone in the dark, praying, while the boat is already miles out and fighting the waves. The detail about the "fourth watch" is worth noting: that is between three and six in the morning, the last watch of the night, the darkest and longest stretch.

When the disciples see him coming toward them across the water, their first response is sheer terror. They think he is a ghost. Jesus speaks before anything else: "Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid." The phrase "it is I" is, in the Greek, literally *ego eimi* — I am — the same construction the Gospel of John uses for Jesus's great self-declarations. Matthew's readers would have caught the echo.

Peter's request is endearing and a little reckless, as Peter usually is. He does not wait to be invited; he wants to be commanded to come. And Jesus says simply, "Come." Peter walks on the water until he notices the wind, and then the noticing is what undoes him. He does not fail because the waves grow stronger; he fails because he looks away from the person who told him to come. Jesus catches him immediately — the word is urgent, instantaneous — and the mild rebuke, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" is asked by someone who is already holding him up. The question does not come before the rescue; it comes after.

**Wound named and hand extended**

What Jeremiah and Matthew share today is this sequence: the honest accounting of what has gone wrong, followed immediately by the act of rescue that does not wait for the person to have deserved it. Israel's wound is real, and God names it — and then restores. Peter's doubt is real, and Jesus names it — and has already caught him. The naming is not the end of the story in either case. It is part of the mercy.

On the memorial of Saint John Vianney, the patron of parish priests, who heard confessions for sixteen and eighteen hours a day and who understood better than most that people come to God already half-sunk, this pairing feels entirely right. He believed that no wound was too old or too deep for what was being offered.

**To carry today**

Think of something in your own life you have been reluctant to name honestly — some pattern, some failure, some fear — because naming it felt like admitting there was no way out. Consider that the naming and the rescue are not opposites. Ask for the grace to say what is true about yourself, because the hand is already extended.

liturgical_day: Monday of the Eighteenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: The false prophet promises comfort; the true one walks into the storm.
reflection:
There is a strange, almost theatrical quality to today's first reading — two prophets, facing each other in the Temple, each claiming to speak for God. And then there is the Gospel, where the disciples look out from a wave-tossed boat at a figure walking toward them across the water and cannot tell whether he is real or a ghost. Both readings, in their different ways, are about the difficulty of recognizing what is actually true when fear and wishful thinking are both tugging hard at us.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 28:1-17**

By the time this scene takes place, Jeremiah has been prophesying for decades, and not one of his words has been pleasant. He has warned of conquest, exile, catastrophe — the consequence of a nation that has turned away from God and put its trust in alliances and idols instead. He has been mocked, imprisoned, and told repeatedly to be quiet. Now, in the fourth year of King Zedekiah's reign — probably around 594 BC, with Babylon's power already crushing and the first wave of exiles already gone — a prophet named Hananiah steps up in the Temple itself and announces that within two years, everything will be reversed. The sacred vessels taken to Babylon will come back. The king taken captive will come home. The yoke of Babylon will be shattered.

It is worth pausing here to feel the pull of Hananiah's message. He is not a fool or a cartoonish villain. He is saying what everyone desperately wants to hear. And he says it in the name of the Lord, with the right formulas, in the right place. How is anyone supposed to know he is wrong?

Jeremiah's response is one of the most quietly devastating moments in all of prophetic literature. He does not shout Hananiah down. He says, essentially, *I hope you're right.* Amen. May God do exactly what you have said. But here is the problem: prophets who predict peace are only confirmed as genuine when the peace actually arrives. And the pattern of the tradition runs the other way — toward warning, toward difficulty, toward the hard word rather than the comfortable one. Hananiah then does something dramatic: he takes the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck — Jeremiah had been walking around wearing an actual yoke as a living parable of Babylonian servitude — and smashes it. A powerful visual. A crowd-pleasing moment. And Jeremiah simply walks away.

The word that comes to Jeremiah afterward is sharp and sad: by breaking the wooden yoke, Hananiah has only guaranteed an iron one. The false mercy that tells people not to prepare for what is coming does not protect them from it; it only ensures they are caught unprepared. And Hananiah dies within the year, the text says, because he has "preached rebellion against the LORD" — not rebellion against the king, but against the God whose hard word Hananiah would not carry.

Psalm 119 sits perfectly in this context. "Remove from me the way of falsehood," it prays, "and favor me with your law." The whole psalm is a long, ardent love song to God's statutes — not because rules are pleasant in themselves, but because they are reliable. They do not shift with the mood of the crowd. The person who clings to them, the psalm says, is not put to shame. Hananiah, who did not cling to them, was.

**The Gospel — Matthew 14:22-36**

The disciples have just witnessed the feeding of the five thousand. You would think they would be steadied by that. Instead they are on a boat in the dark, the wind against them, terrified of a shape moving on the water — and even when Jesus identifies himself, even when Peter manages to step out onto the waves, the moment he looks at the wind, down he goes. The disciples are not failures; they are a very accurate picture of what faith actually looks like in practice: luminous one moment, floundering the next, always closer to shore than they realize.

There is something worth noticing in the detail that Jesus has gone up the mountain alone to pray. He does this after a full, exhausting day. The disciples are in the storm while Jesus is at prayer — and yet it is precisely from that prayer that he comes to them. The two things are not separate.

Peter's cry, "Lord, save me," is barely three words in Greek, and it is enough. The hand reaches out immediately. The mild rebuke — "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" — is less a scolding than a genuine question, almost a philosophical one. What exactly was it that broke the spell? Not the wind itself, but the sight of the wind, the moment attention shifted from the person to the conditions.

**Where falsehood and fear meet**

These two readings are on separate tracks in terms of their narrative worlds — Jeremiah's Temple and the Sea of Galilee have nothing to do with each other historically. But they orbit the same question: what do you trust when things look impossible? Hananiah trusted the story that felt best, and it cost him everything. Peter trusted the wrong thing — the storm — for only a moment, and Christ's hand was already there before he finished sinking. The difference is not that Hananiah was a bad man and Peter was a good one. The difference is that Peter, even sinking, turned toward the right person and asked.

**To carry today**

Think of a place in your life where you are drawn to the comfortable explanation — the one that lets you off the hook, or keeps the situation from being as serious as it might be. It is worth asking honestly whether you are listening for Jeremiah or for Hananiah, for the true word or the welcome one. And when you feel the wind picking up and your footing goes uncertain, notice how quickly help comes when you stop arguing with the storm and simply ask.

epigraph: God feeds a crowd of thousands from almost nothing, and there are twelve baskets left over.
reflection:
There is a particular kind of hunger the world cannot touch — not for lack of trying, but because the world is selling the wrong thing. That is the sharp insight threading through today's readings: that we spend ourselves on what cannot satisfy us, and God keeps offering something else entirely. The invitation is always open, and the bread is always enough.

**The first reading — Isaiah 55:1-3**

This passage opens the fifty-fifth chapter of Isaiah, which is itself the great turning point of what scholars call the Book of Consolation — the second half of Isaiah, written to a people in exile in Babylon. They have been there long enough that exile has started to feel normal. Long enough to begin building lives around substitutes: the small comforts, the local loyalties, the strategies of survival that everyone develops when the real thing feels out of reach.

Into that context, God speaks with an almost startling urgency: *come to the water, come without cost, come and eat.* The language is marketplace language — grain, wine, milk, money, wages — but turned completely inside out. Everything on offer here is free. And the question God asks is not rhetorical; it lands like a genuine puzzle: why are you spending what you have on what cannot satisfy you? The Hebrew behind "fails to satisfy" carries the sense of fullness that never quite arrives, of eating and still being hungry in some deeper way. Israel in Babylon knows exactly what that is like. So do we.

The psalm chosen for today is Psalm 145, and it answers Isaiah directly. "The hand of the Lord feeds us; he answers all our needs." The psalmist is not singing an abstraction — he is stacking images: God opening a hand, eyes lifted hopefully, food given in due season, every living thing satisfied. It is the same feast Isaiah is announcing, seen from the other side. The one who calls you to the banquet is already there waiting.

**The second reading — Romans 8:35, 37-39**

Paul's letter to the Romans is running on its own track here — not commenting on the feeding miracle or on Isaiah directly. He is near the end of a long argument about what it means to live in the Spirit rather than in the flesh, and he lands here at one of the most luminous passages he ever wrote.

The list he gives is worth sitting with: anguish, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, the sword. These are not abstract threats. Paul knows most of them personally, and his first readers know several of them firsthand. He is not waving them away. He is insisting that none of them — not one, not all of them together, not even death — can cut the bond between us and the love of God in Christ. The word he uses for our victory through this is overwhelming, almost excessive. We do not merely survive; we conquer overwhelmingly, which in Greek suggests something closer to a rout than a close win. The love of God is not fragile. It does not need us to be in a good situation to hold.

**The Gospel — Matthew 14:13-21**

Matthew gives us something the other Gospel accounts of this miracle do not begin with: grief. Jesus has just learned that John the Baptist has been executed — his cousin, his forerunner, the one who baptized him. He withdraws by boat to a deserted place. He needs to be alone. And the crowds follow him anyway, on foot, around the shore, arriving before he does.

Here is where Matthew does something quietly remarkable. He does not show us Jesus sighing and bracing himself for the intrusion. He shows us Jesus looking at the crowd and being *moved with pity*. The Greek word for this is one of the strongest in the language — it refers to a physical sensation, something in the gut, a compassion that is felt before it is decided. Jesus is in grief, and he still sees the crowd, and something moves in him, and he heals the sick among them.

By evening, the disciples are practical men doing practical math. There are thousands of people, there is nowhere nearby to buy food, and they have five loaves and two fish. Their suggestion — send them away to fend for themselves — is not cruel; it is just how ordinary human logistics work. Jesus's answer stops them cold: "There is no need for them to go away. Give them some food yourselves." He says this knowing full well what they have. He is not pretending the loaves are more than they are. He is doing something else entirely.

He takes what they offer, looks up to heaven, says the blessing, breaks the loaves, and gives them to the disciples to distribute. The action is unmistakably Eucharistic in its language — take, bless, break, give. Matthew means for us to notice that. What happens next is not explained: five thousand men, plus women and children, eat until they are satisfied, and there are twelve baskets of fragments left over. Twelve — one for each tribe of Israel, one for each disciple. No one goes home hungry. Nothing is wasted.

**Where scarcity becomes abundance**

What connects Isaiah, the psalm, and the feeding of the five thousand is the same movement: God receives what we bring — which is never enough — and from that not-enoughness makes more than enough. Isaiah's exiles have no money and no merit; they come empty-handed and eat well. The crowd in the desert has no provisions; they sit down on the grass and are satisfied. The disciples have almost nothing; they end up carrying away more than they started with.

This is not a lesson in optimism or positive thinking. It is a description of how God actually operates — taking our poverty seriously and then doing something with it that we cannot do ourselves. The one thing required, in Isaiah as in the Gospel, is to come. To bring what you have. To not walk away before the blessing.

**To carry today**

Think of one place in your life where you feel genuinely insufficient — where what you have to offer seems too small for what is being asked of you. Sit with that today not as a problem to solve but as an offering to place in front of God. Ask for the grace to bring it forward anyway, and to let the blessing be his work rather than yours.

liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint Alphonsus Liguori, Bishop and Doctor of the Church
title_main: Saint Alphonsus Liguori, Bishop and Doctor of the Church
epigraph: Two prophets stand before power and tell the truth anyway. One lives; one does not.
reflection:
Today the Church remembers Alphonsus Liguori, an eighteenth-century bishop who spent his life insisting that God's mercy is larger than human fear — that people who feel trapped in their sins are not beyond reach. It is a fitting day for readings about men who tell the truth to dangerous people and pay the price, or nearly pay the price. Both Jeremiah and John the Baptist stand before rulers who have the power to destroy them, and both tell the truth anyway. The shape of their stories is almost identical. The outcomes are not.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 26:11-16, 24**

We are in the temple courts of Jerusalem, which is the last place you might expect to see a mob forming — but here we are. Jeremiah has just delivered what scholars call the "Temple Sermon," a blistering address in which he warned that God would destroy this very temple if the people did not change their ways. That was not what anyone wanted to hear, especially the priests and the professional prophets whose livelihood and prestige depended on the temple standing forever and God being reliably pleased with his people. So they turned on him.

The accusation is stark: *this man deserves death*. Blasphemy, or something very close to it — he has prophesied disaster for the holy city, and in their view that makes him an enemy of God rather than a servant of one. They are certain they are right. That certainty is part of what makes this scene so uncomfortable, because they are not wicked people calculating how to silence a critic; they genuinely believe they are defending the faith.

What Jeremiah does in response is remarkable. He does not argue strategy, does not try to negotiate, does not recant. He simply states the facts: God sent him, the message is real, and if they kill him, they will be killing an innocent man — which means the blood will be on their heads, not his. And then, in what may be the quietest act of courage in the whole book, he says: *as for me, I am in your hands*. Not resignation, and not a death wish — it reads more like a man who has simply decided that the truth is worth whatever comes next.

The crowd turns. Whether from conscience or political calculation or both, the princes conclude that Jeremiah has been speaking in God's name, and that executing prophets who speak in God's name is a path they do not want to start down. A well-placed official named Ahikam shelters him, and he lives.

Psalm 69 is Jeremiah's interior experience set to music — the mire, the flood-waters, the pit about to close. The psalmist cries out from exactly that place of danger, holding on to the conviction that *the Lord hears the poor, and his own who are in bonds he spurns not*. Prayed after this reading, it sounds like what Jeremiah might have whispered to himself in the courtyard while waiting to find out whether he would live or die.

**The Gospel — Matthew 14:1-12**

The Gospel tells a story that ends very differently. John the Baptist has been arrested by Herod Antipas, a client-king ruling a portion of what had been his father's territory, on account of a similarly inconvenient truth: John had said publicly that Herod's marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, was unlawful. He was right, and Herod knew it, which is why Herod feared him and would not simply have him killed — the people regarded John as a prophet, and prophets had a way of mattering to crowds.

The birthday banquet is the mechanism of catastrophe. The daughter of Herodias dances, Herod makes a reckless oath in front of his guests, and Herodias sees her moment. She has her daughter ask for the Baptist's head on a platter. Matthew notes that Herod was distressed — and that detail is important, because this is not a monster at ease with what he is about to do. He is a weak man, trapped by his own boasting and his fear of looking weak in front of people who are watching. He orders the execution anyway.

That is what makes this episode so specific and so grim. Herod knows better. His distress is a moral signal he overrides. The machinery of vanity and peer pressure and political calculation does what it does, and John dies in prison, and his disciples bury him and go tell Jesus.

**What mercy looks like under pressure**

These two readings are on separate tracks in the sense that they were chosen independently — the Jeremiah passage runs through a lectionary cycle while the Gospel is assigned to this week in Matthew. But they arrive at the same place. In both, a man speaks truth to power. In both, the one in power has a choice. Jeremiah's judges choose rightly, if narrowly. Herod does not. The difference is not intelligence or even goodwill — Herod seems to have had more of both than the priests who wanted Jeremiah dead. The difference is whether a man can bear to be seen doing what he knows is right when it costs him something publicly.

Alphonsus Liguori spent his life in moral theology, which is the Church's ongoing effort to think carefully about exactly these human moments — the pressure, the oath, the crowd, the distress that gets overridden. He was particularly interested in people who felt unworthy of mercy, and he kept insisting that mercy was not a reward for the strong. The readings today, in their way, show him what he was working with.

**To carry today**

Think of a moment recently when you knew the right thing and the crowd — or the room, or the mood of the evening — pulled you the other way. Not a dramatic choice like Herod's, but the ordinary version: the true thing left unsaid, the correction quietly swallowed. Ask for the honesty to name it to yourself, and the trust that naming it honestly is already the beginning of something better.

liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Priest
epigraph: The prophet speaks what he is given, and the crowd reaches for his throat.
reflection:
There is a pattern running through today's readings that anyone who has ever said something true and unwelcome will recognize immediately. Jeremiah stands in the temple courtyard and delivers a message he did not choose, and by the time he finishes speaking, his audience is ready to kill him. Jesus returns to his own hometown and teaches in the synagogue, and the people who knew him as a child cannot get past the fact that they knew him as a child. The messenger is rejected because the message is too close, too inconvenient, too disruptive of what people have already decided to believe. On the feast of Ignatius of Loyola — a man who upended his entire life to follow a call he hadn't expected — this pattern carries a particular charge.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 26:1-9**

This passage opens a new section of Jeremiah, sometimes called the "temple sermon." We are at the very beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, probably around 608 BC, a moment of serious political anxiety in Judah. Babylon is rising. Egypt has just killed Jehoiakim's predecessor. The people are frightened, and the temple — the great symbol of God's presence and protection — is their reassurance. The Lord tells Jeremiah to go and stand in the temple court and speak everything he is commanded, and to omit nothing. That phrase is worth sitting with: *omit nothing*. Jeremiah is not given the freedom to soften the hard parts.

The substance of what he says is this: if the people do not turn back, the temple will become like Shiloh. Shiloh was where the Ark of the Covenant had been kept before the Philistines captured it — a sanctuary so thoroughly destroyed that its name had become shorthand for total devastation. To say the Jerusalem temple would become like Shiloh was to say the unthinkable out loud, in the temple itself, in front of the priests. It was roughly the equivalent of walking into a packed cathedral and announcing that God was going to reduce it to rubble. The reaction is predictable and immediate: the priests and the prophets — the professional religious class, the people whose authority and livelihood are bound up in this institution — seize Jeremiah and shout that he must die.

What makes the scene so painful is that Jeremiah is not there as an enemy. He is sent with a "perhaps" — *perhaps they will listen and turn back*. The message is simultaneously a threat and an appeal. God has not written these people off yet; the whole point of the prophet's errand is to create one more opening for repentance. But the messenger is grabbed before the message can land.

Psalm 69 answers this moment with an almost uncanny directness. It is the prayer of someone who is suffering unjustly for God's sake: surrounded by enemies without cause, cast out, bearing insults that were aimed at God and landed on the one who spoke for God. "Zeal for your house consumes me," the psalm says — and that line from the psalmist will later be applied to Jesus himself as he cleanses the temple. The psalm is not a tidy resolution; it is the raw cry of someone in the middle of it, still praying, still turning toward God even while the trap closes.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:54-58**

Jesus comes back to Nazareth. Matthew tells us the people in the synagogue were astonished — and then immediately explains why their astonishment curdled into offense. They begin listing what they know about him: the carpenter's son, Mary's boy, brother of James and Joseph and Simon and Judas, whose sisters are right here among us. Every item on the list is true. None of it is wrong. And yet the very familiarity that should make them trust him — we know this man, we watched him grow up — becomes the reason they cannot receive him. They have already filed him away. He doesn't fit in the drawer they've opened.

Jesus responds with a saying that reads almost like a rueful observation rather than a rebuke: a prophet is without honor in his native place and in his own household. He is not surprised. He has, apparently, encountered this before. What is quietly devastating is the line that follows: he did not work many mighty deeds there because of their lack of faith. Not that he refused out of spite, but that faith and healing are not two separate events — the openness to receive is itself part of how grace works. A closed hand cannot take hold of what is being offered.

**What the prophet costs**

These two readings are not on separate tracks today; they are telling exactly the same story from two different moments in salvation history. The prophet speaks the word of God, the hearers cannot bear it, and the community that should have been most receptive — the one closest to the source — is the one most determined to silence him. Jeremiah's neighbors grab him in the temple court. Jesus' neighbors take offense in the synagogue. In both cases, proximity breeds not faith but a particular kind of stubbornness, the stubbornness of people who have already decided what God looks like and are not prepared to be corrected.

Ignatius of Loyola knew something about this. He was a soldier who had his leg shattered by a cannonball and spent his convalescence reading the lives of the saints — the only books on offer — and found, to his considerable surprise, that they moved him in a way that his fantasies of military glory did not. He eventually founded the Society of Jesus and sent men across the known world to preach and teach, often into communities that did not want them. He understood that the word given to you is not always the word that will be welcomed, and that this is not a reason to omit it.

**To carry today**

Think today about something true that you have held back because the person in front of you has already made up their mind, or because the relationship felt too close to risk. Is there something you are being called to say — or to hear — that you have been quietly filing away because you know how it will be received? Ask for the courage to neither silence the word nor harden against it.

liturgical_day: Thursday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: The potter does not discard the clay — he works it again, into what he pleases.
reflection:
There is a theme running through today's two readings that you could call patience, but that word is too thin. What the potter and the fisherman both embody is something closer to an unhurried authority — a willingness to work all the way to the end before declaring what anything is. That is a difficult posture to trust from the inside of the clay, or from inside the net. But it is the posture these readings ask us to consider.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 18:1-6**

Jeremiah is writing from one of the darkest periods in Israel's history — the decades before the Babylonian exile, when the kingdom is rotting from within and the prophets who say so are, for their trouble, threatened and thrown in cisterns. God has been sending Jeremiah word after word of warning, and the people have largely not listened. Into this grinding situation comes one of Scripture's most vivid domestic images: go down to the potter's house.

So Jeremiah goes. And what he sees is utterly ordinary — a craftsman at his wheel, hands wet with clay, shaping something. And then the clay goes wrong. It collapses or warps or simply refuses the shape the potter intended. And without dramatics, without discarding the lump and starting fresh with new material, the potter simply *tries again*. Same clay, different form, same patient hands.

The word God gives Jeremiah out of this scene is worth sitting with. It is not a threat, exactly, though it has been read as one. "Can I not do to you, house of Israel, as this potter has done?" The question is rhetorical, but it cuts both ways. Yes, God has the authority of the potter over the clay. That is real and should not be softened. But the image also contains mercy: the potter does not throw the clay away. He reworks it. The clay that went wrong is still in his hands. He is still at the wheel.

Psalm 146 answers this reading by naming where reliable help actually comes from. The psalm has a gentle edge of warning — do not trust princes, because even the best of them die and their plans die with them — but its real motion is toward praise. Blessed is the one whose hope is in the God of Jacob: the God who made everything, who keeps faith forever. That "keeps faith forever" lands differently after Jeremiah's potter. The hands at the wheel do not tire.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:47-53**

This is the last in a string of parables Matthew has been running through chapter 13 — the sower, the wheat and weeds, the mustard seed, the yeast, the hidden treasure, the pearl of great price. The net parable is in some ways the simplest: a dragnet is thrown into the sea, it pulls in everything, and only at the shore is the sorting done.

What the parable insists on is the timing. The separation does not happen in the water. The net does not discriminate while it is being dragged; it catches every kind. The judgment — what is good, what is thrown away — happens at the end, on the shore, when the work is finished. Jesus is explicit that this is a picture of the end of the age, not a picture of human sorting in the present.

The brief exchange that follows is easy to rush past. Jesus asks, "Do you understand all these things?" and the disciples say yes — which, given how consistently confused they have been throughout this gospel, is a little bit funny and a little bit touching. Jesus does not contradict them. Instead he gives them one more image: the scribe who has been instructed in the Kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings from the storeroom both the new and the old. Something is being passed to them, something they are now responsible for carrying forward.

**The patience that runs through both readings**

These two passages are on separate tracks in the sense that Jeremiah and Matthew have nothing directly to do with each other. But they are pressing on the same question from different sides: when does the final shape of things become clear?

Jeremiah's potter answers: not while the clay is still wet. You do not know what the vessel will be until the hands have finished their work. The net parable answers: not while everything is still in the water. The sorting is real, but it belongs to the end, not the middle. Both images place the reader — place us — firmly in the middle, and both ask for a trust that is not the same as passivity. The clay does not resist the hands. The fish do not try to sort themselves.

There is something genuinely consoling here for anyone who is in a season of waiting or confusion or incompleteness, and also something genuinely sobering for anyone who has decided the work is finished and the sorting already done. The potter is still at the wheel. The net is still being dragged. The end has not yet come to the shore.

**To carry today**

Think of somewhere in your life where you have decided a person — or a situation, or yourself — is finished goods, already sorted, beyond further working. Ask whether that judgment is yours to make, or whether the potter is simply not done yet. Hold a little looseness there today, and see what that opens up.

liturgical_day: Memorial of Saints Martha, Mary, and Lazarus
epigraph: Martha walks out to meet Jesus in the road and names him Lord before the tomb is even opened.
reflection:
Today the Church celebrates three people who are not apostles, not martyrs, not founders of anything — just a family in Bethany that loved Jesus and received him into their home. That is the whole reason they are here. The feast was long observed in some parts of the Church, but in 2021 it was placed on the universal calendar, which is the Church's way of saying: this kind of love is worth commemorating everywhere.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 15:10, 16-21**

This passage comes from what scholars call Jeremiah's "confessions" — a series of raw, almost shockingly personal complaints the prophet makes directly to God. Jeremiah is not a happy man. He is preaching doom to a people who do not want to hear it, and the cost is social isolation, hostility, and what sounds like serious spiritual exhaustion. He was called to speak before he was born, and by this point in the book he seems to regret that the deal was ever struck.

What makes the passage so striking is the way it swings between two registers. In the first movement, Jeremiah says he *devoured* God's words when he found them — they were his joy, his happiness, the thing that made his life feel alive and purposeful. This is not a man who came to prophecy reluctantly. He wanted it. The words were sweet. But the sweetness has curdled. Now he is sitting alone, under the weight of God's hand, filled with indignation he cannot put down, and the God who gave him the words has started to feel like a treacherous brook — a wadi that looks like a reliable stream and then, in the dry season, simply disappears.

That image of the dry wadi is one of the grimmer metaphors in the whole prophetic tradition. In a desert landscape, finding a brook that has gone dry when you were counting on it is not a minor disappointment. It is potentially lethal. Jeremiah is accusing God, gently but unmistakably, of being the thing he most needed and finding it gone when he arrived.

God's answer is not an apology. It is more like a reorientation: if you repent and come back, you will stand before me; if you can separate the precious from the worthless, you will speak for me again; and I will make you a brass wall that they cannot break. The promise is not comfort exactly — it is a commission renewed, which is what Jeremiah actually needs. The psalm chosen for the day echoes this: *God is my refuge on the day of distress.* Psalm 59 is the prayer of someone genuinely surrounded by enemies, and its refrain is not "everything is fine" but rather "you have been my stronghold even so."

**The Gospel — John 11:19-27**

The lectionary gives two options today. The first, from John 11, is the more theologically weighty, and it is the one worth sitting with longest.

Lazarus is already dead. The mourners are already at the house. Martha hears Jesus is coming and does something remarkable: she goes out to meet him on the road, before he reaches the house, before the tomb is opened, before anything has happened. It is an act of initiative that the text clearly wants us to notice, because it contrasts immediately with Mary, who stays home.

What Martha says when she reaches him is not simply complaint, though it begins there — "if you had been here, my brother would not have died." Anyone who has ever prayed urgently for something that did not happen will recognize that sentence. But Martha does not stop there. She adds, without being prompted: *"But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you."* She is grieving and she still believes. Those two things are sitting side by side in her, and she is not trying to resolve the tension.

When Jesus tells her "your brother will rise," she hears it the way any educated first-century Jew would: resurrection on the last day, the general resurrection that the Pharisees affirmed and the Sadducees denied. It is orthodox, it is true, and it is not quite what Jesus means. And so he corrects her — not harshly, but with precision: *"I am the resurrection and the life."* Not a resurrection that will happen. Not even a resurrection he will bring about. The resurrection is him, present, standing in front of her in the road.

Then the question: *"Do you believe this?"* Martha's answer is one of the great confessions of the Gospel of John. She does not say she fully understands it. She says she believes he is the Christ, the Son of God, the one coming into the world. This is the same formula the whole Gospel is written to produce in its readers. Martha gets there on a dusty road outside Bethany, in the middle of her grief, before the miracle.

**A family and a prophet, both holding on**

The connection between Jeremiah and Martha is not an obvious one, but it is real. Both of them are people who received something — the word of God, the friendship of God — and found that it cost more than they expected. Both of them continue anyway, not because the suffering has been explained to them, but because the one they are speaking to is still present. Jeremiah devoured the words and then felt abandoned; Martha's brother died while Jesus was somewhere else. Neither of them walks away. That persistence is not cheerful or tidy, but it is faith, and the readings together suggest that God takes that kind of faith seriously.

**To carry today**

Think of a place in your life where you prayed with genuine urgency and the answer did not come the way you hoped — where God felt, for a time, like that dry brook. Notice whether you are still standing in the road, like Martha, or have drifted back inside the house. You do not have to resolve the grief; you only have to stay close enough to speak.

liturgical_day: Tuesday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: A nation confesses it has nothing left but the name of God to appeal to.
reflection:
There is a particular kind of prayer that comes only after everything else has failed — not a polished petition, but a cry from the rubble. Jeremiah's voice in the first reading and the disciples' quiet question in the Gospel have almost nothing to do with each other on the surface, and it is worth being honest about that. These two are running on separate tracks today. But each, in its own way, is asking for the same thing: to understand what God is doing in a world that looks, from where we stand, like a wreck.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 14:17-22**

This passage comes from a stretch of Jeremiah sometimes called the "drought liturgy" — a sequence of laments, divine responses, and communal prayers organized around a devastating drought and military catastrophe that fell on Judah in the final decades before the Babylonian exile. By chapter fourteen, the prophet has already heard God refuse to be moved by sacrifices and prayers offered insincerely. What we get here is almost unbearable: Jeremiah is told to weep without rest. He goes out to the fields and sees the dead. He goes into the city and sees the starving. Even the priests and prophets — the people who were supposed to have access to God — are wandering in a land they no longer recognize.

The poem turns, about halfway through, from description to confession. "We recognize, O Lord, our wickedness, the guilt of our fathers; that we have sinned against you." This is significant because throughout the book of Jeremiah, the people have been slow to admit anything. They have been blaming the drought on the wrong gods, turning to foreign alliances, telling themselves that the Temple's presence in Jerusalem guaranteed their safety regardless of how they lived. The confession here is real, and it is desperate.

Then comes what is, for my money, one of the strangest and most moving arguments in all of scripture. The people essentially say to God: among all the idols of the nations, not one of them can produce rain. The heavens themselves cannot send showers on their own. You alone have done all these things — which means you alone can undo them. They are not appealing to their own goodness, because they have just admitted they have none. They are appealing to God's name — to the fact that God is who God is, and that a God who abandons his people entirely would be a different God than the one who made the covenant. It is an argument built entirely from rubble, and it is oddly persuasive.

Psalm 79 is the perfect answer to this reading, because it is not an answer — it is a continuation. It carries the same confession, the same appeal to God's name rather than to human merit, and the same raw honesty about how low things have gotten. "For the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us." When the congregation sings this refrain back, they are praying with Jeremiah, which is exactly what the liturgy intends.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:36-43**

The disciples have just heard the parable of the wheat and the weeds — the story of a farmer whose good crop is infiltrated by a weed (almost certainly darnel, a plant that looks exactly like wheat in its early stages and whose roots are so intertwined with wheat that you cannot pull it up without taking the wheat too). The disciples are not satisfied with the story; they want the key. So Jesus goes inside, they follow him, and he gives them the decoded version, term by term.

The explanation is more alarming than the parable. The weeds are real, the enemy who sows them is real, and the final reckoning is real — a fiery furnace, wailing and grinding of teeth. Jesus does not soften this. He is not being cruel; he is being honest with people who are about to go out into a world that will resist everything they preach. But the last image is not fire. It is light: "the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father." That line deserves to sit for a moment. Not that they will be rewarded, not that they will be safe — that they will *shine*. The image is startling and beautiful, a kind of transfiguration of ordinary faithful life.

Notice also what Jesus does *not* say. He does not tell the disciples to start identifying the weeds. That work belongs to the angels, at the end of the age. The implication is that our job is not sorting — it is growing.

**What patience costs**

If there is a thread between these two readings, it is the cost of waiting. Jeremiah's community is waiting for peace that doesn't come and healing that is replaced by terror. The disciples are asking, implicitly, why the weeds are still there. Both are sitting in conditions that look like abandonment.

The answer the liturgy offers — not loudly, but steadily — is that God's timing is not negligence. Jeremiah's people are held to confession and to the covenant. The disciples are held to trust in a final justice that is not theirs to administer. Both are asked to continue in conditions of uncertainty, which is exactly what faith looks like most days.

**To carry today**

Think about some situation in your life where you are waiting for God to act — a relationship that hasn't healed, a prayer that seems to go nowhere, some injustice that keeps standing. Ask yourself honestly: am I still willing to appeal to God's name, even when I have nothing else to offer? Notice whether your prayer today can be honest enough to sound like Jeremiah's.

liturgical_day: Monday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: A rotted loincloth and a mustard seed: God works in the concrete and the small.
reflection:
Today's readings are, on the surface, doing two very different things. Jeremiah is staging a grim object lesson about a nation that has drifted away from God, while Matthew's Jesus is sketching the Kingdom in quick, almost playful images. These two are largely on separate tracks — the prophet's grief and the parables' quiet confidence belong to different moments in salvation history. But there is a thread worth noticing, not forced but real: God keeps working through the ordinary and the material, through cloth and seeds and flour, refusing to stay abstract.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 13:1-11**

We are early in the book of Jeremiah, in the section scholars call his "symbolic actions" — moments when the prophet is asked to *do* something strange in public, or in private, as a kind of living parable. He has already smashed a clay pot at the city gate. Now he is told to buy a linen loincloth, wear it for a time without washing it, then walk to the Parath and bury it in a rock cleft. He waits. He goes back. He digs it up. It is ruined, rotted through, completely useless.

The word translated "loincloth" here is important: this is not a belt or a sash but an undergarment, the piece of clothing worn closest to the body. When God says that Israel and Judah were meant to cling to him the way this garment clings to a man's body, the image is intimate to the point of being almost startling. This is not the language of alliance or covenant obligation in its legal sense — it is the language of closeness, of belonging, of being bound to another by habit and proximity and daily life. They were supposed to be his *people, his renown, his praise, his beauty.* Those are words of pride, even of delight.

And then they did not listen. The loincloth, buried in the earth and left there through neglect, rots. It becomes good for nothing. That, says God through Jeremiah, is what has happened to the people who were meant to wear his name.

The responsorial psalm is drawn from the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy — one of the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible — and it answers Jeremiah with almost the same ache. "You were unmindful of the Rock that begot you, you forgot the God who gave you birth." The word "forgot" is doing heavy lifting there. This is not the forgetting of ignorance; it is the forgetting that comes from distraction, from slowly looking elsewhere until the original face has gone dim.

There is something almost darkly comic about God's response in the psalm — "I will provoke them with a 'no-people'; with a foolish nation I will anger them." God will use their own method against them: they have given their devotion to a "no-god," to idols that are hollow, and so he will stir their jealousy through a people they would not bother to notice. Even the divine grief has a kind of exasperated wit to it.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:31-35**

Matthew 13 is the great parable chapter, and we have been moving through it for several days now. Jesus has already explained the sower and the wheat and the weeds. Now he offers two shorter parables, each barely a sentence long, and each turning on something almost laughably small becoming inexplicably large.

The mustard seed was proverbial in Jewish teaching as the smallest measurable thing — so small it was nearly invisible when held in the palm. Yet in the right conditions it grows into a plant large enough for birds to nest in. The yeast parable works the same way from the opposite direction: a woman folds a small amount of leaven into a large amount of flour — three measures is closer to fifty pounds than to a dinner quantity — and it works through the whole batch invisibly, from within.

Matthew tells us that Jesus spoke only in parables to the crowds, and he ties this to Psalm 78: "I will open my mouth in parables, I will announce what has lain hidden from the foundation of the world." There is something Jesus wants to say about the Kingdom that cannot be said directly, only shown sideways, through images that do their work slowly, the way yeast does.

**Where smallness is the point**

The connection worth sitting with today is this: both readings take God's activity seriously in the particular and the physical. Jeremiah is not given a vision or a dream; he is told to walk to the market, buy cloth, wear it, and get his hands dirty in a rock cleft beside the river. Jesus does not describe the Kingdom as a theological category; he points to a seed and a woman at work in her kitchen.

The loincloth and the mustard seed are not decorations hung on an idea. They are the idea. God works in the material world, through the concrete, the daily, the embarrassingly small. The tragedy in Jeremiah is that Israel looked past the tangible gifts — the land, the law, the daily provision — toward the spectacle of the idols. The hope in Matthew is that the Kingdom is already at work in what looks like nothing, doing what yeast does: changing everything from inside.

**To carry today**

Consider where in your own life you are waiting for the large and obvious sign while something small has already been placed in front of you — a returning habit of prayer, a small act of patience, an almost-invisible change in how you treat someone. Ask whether you have the patience to let the hidden thing do its quiet work.

epigraph: Solomon asks for one thing; the merchant sells everything — both know what is worth wanting.
reflection:
There is a particular kind of clarity that comes over a person when they finally know what they want. Not what they want to want, not what they think they should want — but the thing itself, seen plain, and recognized as worth any cost. Today's readings circle this experience from different angles, and together they raise a question worth sitting with all week: do I actually know what I am looking for?

**The first reading — 1 Kings 3:5, 7-12**

This passage arrives early in the reign of Solomon, David's son, and the scene is a dream. God appears and offers Solomon anything — which is the kind of sentence that stops you cold when you read it slowly. *Anything.* The offer is real; this is not a riddle or a test of nerve. It is a blank check extended to a new king who has just inherited the most powerful throne in the region and who, by his own admission, is young, uncertain, and overwhelmed.

What follows is one of the most quietly remarkable moments in the Hebrew scriptures. Solomon does not ask for long life, or wealth, or victory over his enemies — the three things a sensible advisor would have told him to want. Instead he asks for an understanding heart. The Hebrew behind that phrase suggests something closer to a *listening* heart, a heart that can hear what a situation truly requires, not just what it appears to require on the surface. He wants to be able to tell right from wrong in the complex, tangled, human business of governing real people with real grievances.

God's pleasure at this response is explicit and almost touching. Because Solomon did not ask for the things he could reasonably have wanted — and which God would presumably have granted — he receives something rarer. A wisdom so deep that, the text says, no one before him had it and no one after him will equal it.

Psalm 119 answers this directly. It is the great long psalm of love for God's law, and the verses chosen today strike exactly the same note: the psalmist prizes God's commands above silver and gold. Not as a pious sentiment, but as a tested judgment — the law gives light, gives direction, gives life. The psalm and the first reading together are making a claim: that wisdom, properly understood, is not a human achievement but a gift that flows from loving what God loves.

**The second reading — Romans 8:28-30**

Paul's letter to the Romans is moving, in these middle chapters, through a dense and beautiful argument about what God has been doing in human history — and in individual human lives — from the very beginning. These three verses are among the most consoling in the entire New Testament, and they are also, if you look at them straight, among the most dizzying. Paul strings together a chain of verbs — foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified — and each one carries the weight of a whole theology. He is not promising that good things will happen to people who love God; he is saying that the whole sweep of a life, including its hard and confusing stretches, is held inside a purpose larger than any single moment can reveal.

This reading is on its own track today, in the sense that it does not tie neatly into the images of the kingdom from Solomon and Matthew. But it sets a frame around them. If God's call and purpose are as comprehensive as Paul says, then the longing Solomon feels for wisdom, and the longing the merchant feels for the pearl, are not random. They are part of something being worked out from a direction we cannot fully see.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:44-52**

This is the third and final Sunday in Matthew's great parable chapter, and Jesus offers three parables here in quick succession. The treasure hidden in a field, the pearl of great price, and the net — and then a small coda about the scribe who is like a householder drawing from a storeroom both old things and new.

The treasure and the pearl are often read as a pair, and they are, but they have a subtle difference that is worth noticing. The man who finds the treasure stumbles on it — he was not searching for it specifically; it was just there, in a field he happened to be working. The merchant, on the other hand, is a professional seeker. He has been looking for fine pearls his whole career. One man finds by accident; the other finds by long, intentional search. But the response is identical: both sell *everything* they have, and do so with what the text quietly calls joy. This is not anguish or sacrifice in the tragic sense. It is the relief of a person who has finally found the thing that makes all other things make sense, and who parts with them not grudgingly but gladly.

The net parable that follows is darker — it acknowledges that not everything hauled in is worth keeping, and that a sorting will come. Jesus is not letting his disciples off the hook entirely. But notice that he ends not with the sorting but with the scribe and the storeroom: the one who has learned the kingdom draws on everything, old wisdom and new revelation alike, and finds use for all of it.

**What wisdom costs — and what it frees**

Solomon gives up the easier asks. The merchant gives up his inventory. What both gain in return is not a thing they can hoard but a capacity — to see rightly, to judge rightly, to know what matters. That is the connection the readings are making: real wisdom is recognizable by what it makes a person willing to release. The man who clutches his gold and his silver and his long life at the expense of understanding has not made a wise trade. He has made the trade of someone who does not yet know what the field contains.

**To carry today**

Think about what you are actually asking for when you pray — what you hope for, what you would choose if the choice were laid bare. Are those the things that would make you more capable of love, more able to see what is right, more free? That is not a rebuke; it is an honest question worth bringing to the quiet of the day.

epigraph: A mother asks for thrones; Jesus offers a cup — and James drinks it.
reflection:
James, the son of Zebedee, was martyred by Herod Agrippa around the year 44, making him the first of the Twelve to die for the faith. He left behind no letter, no Gospel, no recorded sermon. What we have instead is a story about his mother asking for the wrong thing on his behalf, and the quiet fact that when the cup came around, he drank it. The Church keeps his feast in red, the color of blood, and the readings she gives him are not comfortable ones.

**The first reading — 2 Corinthians 4:7-15**

Paul is writing to a community that has started to doubt him. His opponents have apparently argued that a genuine apostle wouldn't look so battered — wouldn't be so often imprisoned, hungry, shipwrecked, or afraid. Real authority, they suggest, would be more impressive. Paul's response is one of the most quietly stunning passages in all his letters: yes, exactly, that is precisely the point. The treasure — meaning the gospel, the knowledge of God revealed in Christ — is being carried in earthen vessels, which is the Greek way of saying clay pots. Ordinary, breakable, worth almost nothing in themselves.

The image would have landed hard for Paul's original readers, because clay jars were everywhere in the ancient world and they were understood to be temporary containers. You did not treasure a clay jar; you treasured what was inside it. Paul is saying that the apostle himself is the clay jar. His weakness, his suffering, his very un-glamorous appearance is not evidence against his mission but evidence of where the power actually comes from.

What follows is a string of paradoxes so carefully balanced they feel almost like a creed: afflicted but not constrained, perplexed but not despairing, struck down but not destroyed. Each pair holds the weight without resolving it — Paul is not saying the suffering doesn't hurt, he is saying it doesn't have the last word. And the reason is specific: he is "always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus." This is not metaphor for Paul; it is a literal description of what apostolic life has cost him. The death is real. But so is the logic that follows — if the dying of Jesus is present in the body, then the life of Jesus may also be manifested there.

Psalm 126 sits alongside this with its image of those who go out weeping, carrying seed, and come back carrying sheaves. The psalm was originally about the return from exile in Babylon — the shock of captives discovering, almost disbelieving, that they were going home. Paul is living inside exactly that movement: the exile of suffering, the homecoming of resurrection.

**The Gospel — Matthew 20:20-28**

There is something genuinely touching about the mother of James and John marching up to Jesus and asking for the best seats in the Kingdom. Matthew gives us the mother as the speaker; Mark has the brothers ask directly themselves. Either way, the request is the same and the embarrassment is the same — she wants her boys on the right and left of Jesus when he comes into his glory.

Jesus doesn't mock her for it. He turns and speaks to the sons: "Can you drink the chalice that I am going to drink?" And they say, without hesitation, that they can. They almost certainly have no idea what they are agreeing to. They are thinking about glory; he is thinking about Gethsemane. But here is what the Church holds onto on this feast day: they said yes, and eventually they meant it. James would be beheaded. The cup would come, and he would drink it — not because he was fearless, but because he had said yes to something larger than he understood.

Jesus then gathers all twelve and explains what authority is going to look like among them. The Gentile rulers lord it over their subjects; greatness among the disciples is to work the other way entirely — the greatest is the servant, the first is the slave. And then the sentence that grounds all of it: the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. He is not issuing a rule about church governance in the abstract. He is describing himself, and he is saying: be like this.

**Ambition turned inside out**

What holds these readings together is the question of what power is actually for. The mother wants her sons elevated; Paul is writing from a posture of radical diminishment; James ends up executed. The trajectory of the Gospel is not upward mobility but downward service — and not because suffering is good in itself, but because something gets through in the broken places that cannot get through any other way. Paul's clay jar carries the treasure precisely because the jar doesn't get in the way. James's death bore witness to something no living comfortable apostle could have said quite so clearly.

This is not a comfortable feast. But it is an honest one, and there is something freeing about the honesty. The Church is not asking us to be more impressive. She is asking us to be more available — to what is being poured in, and to where it needs to go.

**To carry today**

Think of something you are carrying right now that feels like pure loss — a situation that has cost you something and shows no sign of producing anything. Ask whether it might, despite appearances, be one of those places where something is getting through that couldn't get through any other way. You don't have to feel that yet. Just stay open to the possibility that the jar being broken is not the end of the story.

liturgical_day: Friday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: God gathers the scattered; the question is what kind of soil we give him to work with.
reflection:
Two passages, one from the prophet and one from the Lord himself, and they are not quite on the same track — Jeremiah is speaking of exile and return, and Jesus is explaining a parable about hearing. But they rhyme in a way that is worth noticing: both are about what happens when the word of God actually lands somewhere, and both are quietly urgent about it.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 3:14-17**

By the time we reach chapter three of Jeremiah, the prophet has already laid out the charge against Israel at some length. The people have been unfaithful — not in some vague spiritual sense, but in the specific, political, religious chaos of the late seventh century before Christ, when the nation was hemorrhaging its allegiance to God and patching it back together with idols and foreign alliances. The tone of the opening chapters is by turns indignant and heartbroken, and what makes Jeremiah remarkable is that the heartbreak belongs not just to the prophet but to God himself. The LORD speaks in this book the way a husband speaks of a wife who has left — not coldly, not with bureaucratic judgment, but with a grief that keeps reasserting itself even in the accusation.

So when verse 14 opens with "Return, rebellious children," the word "rebellious" in the original carries something like the idea of turning away, of an about-face in the wrong direction. And yet the sentence doesn't end in punishment — it ends in gathering. "I will take you, one from a city, two from a clan, and bring you to Zion." That image is worth sitting with: not a mass return, not a parade, but a patient individual rescue — one person here, two families there — as though God is going house to house. The numbers suggest a remnant, a small and scattered group, not a triumphant national restoration. But the tenderness is in the detail.

Then comes something startling. The LORD says that in those coming days, people will no longer speak of the ark of the covenant, no longer miss it or look for it or try to rebuild it. For Israel, the ark was the most sacred object in existence — the gold-covered chest housing the tablets of the law, the physical sign of God's presence with the people. Its loss to the Babylonians was catastrophic. And yet here God says: don't worry about the ark. Jerusalem itself will be called the LORD's throne. The presence of God will not be contained in an object; it will fill the city, and through the city, draw all nations. It is a promise so large it is almost hard to absorb — an end to the exile of the heart, not just the exile from the land.

The psalm, drawn from Jeremiah 31 rather than from Psalms, sings this same hope back in a warmer register: the scattered are gathered, mourning turns to joy, the young and the old dance together. It is the same promise sung rather than declared.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:18-23**

This is not the parable of the sower itself — that came the day before, and the disciples asked Jesus what it meant. This is Jesus answering. It is a rare thing in the Gospels: an explicit, point-by-point interpretation given by Jesus himself. Usually he leaves the parables open, lets them work in the listener. Here he closes the loop, probably because the disciples have asked directly and because he trusts them with more than the crowd receives.

The fourfold soil — the hard path, the rocky ground, the thorny patch, the good earth — maps onto four kinds of hearing. What is striking is that three of the four actually receive the word. The seed falls. The problem in most cases is not that the word is absent but that something prevents it from taking root: incomprehension in the first case, shallow enthusiasm without depth in the second, the slow suffocation of anxiety and wealth in the third. Only the last hearer both receives and understands — and the verb "understands" here is doing real work. It doesn't mean intellectual mastery; it means something closer to taking in, absorbing, letting the word become part of how you see and act.

The yields — a hundred, sixty, thirtyfold — are agricultural extravagances. A Palestinian farmer would have been delighted with a tenfold return. Jesus is describing not merely adequate fruit but abundance.

**Hearing as homecoming**

What connects Jeremiah and Matthew today is not a shared image but a shared question: what does it take for the word of God to actually arrive? Jeremiah's God is gathering a scattered people one by one — it is an act of pure initiative, God doing the seeking. Jesus describes the word going out like seed, falling on every kind of ground — that too is God's initiative, prodigal and unprejudiced. But in both cases, something is required on the receiving end. The scattered have to be willing to return; the soil has to be what it is.

Jeremiah promises that God will appoint shepherds "after my own heart" to tend the gathered people wisely. The psalm echoes it: the Lord himself is the shepherd who guards the flock. And in Matthew, the word that the good-soil hearer receives and understands is precisely the word of the Kingdom — the news that the shepherd is here, that the gathering has begun, that even now the seed is going out.

The invitation is not to anxiety about which soil we are. It is to notice whether we are actually hearing.

**To carry today**

Think about where your attention goes when you sit with something difficult — a scripture reading, a conversation you didn't want to have, a question about your own life. Do you absorb it, or does something else quickly crowd it out? Ask today for one moment of genuine attention, of letting something you hear actually land and stay.

liturgical_day: Thursday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: God remembers the love of the beginning, and keeps offering the living water we keep refusing.
reflection:
There is a marriage gone wrong at the heart of today's first reading, and a crowd that cannot quite see what is standing right in front of them in the Gospel. Both are stories about a strange and persistent blindness — the kind that is not accidental but chosen, not a failure of information but a failure of desire. What makes these readings worth sitting with is that neither God nor Jesus gives up because of it.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 2:1-3, 7-8, 12-13**

Jeremiah is one of the great tragic figures of the Hebrew scriptures. He prophesied for decades in Jerusalem before its fall to Babylon in 587 B.C., watching the city ignore warning after warning. What we have today is almost the opening of his public ministry — a kind of prosecution speech delivered on God's behalf to the city. It is worth knowing that the speech is not angry in the way we might expect. It opens with something closer to grief.

God recalls the early days of Israel's relationship with him — the desert years, the wilderness wandering after the Exodus. That period was not, historically, a golden age in any simple sense; the wilderness stories are full of complaint and rebellion. But the image here reaches past the historical record toward something true in another register: there was a time of nearness, of dependence, of being carried. "I remember the devotion of your youth," God says, "how you loved me as a bride." The marriage metaphor would have been startling when Jeremiah first spoke it, and it remains startling. The God of the universe is describing himself as a husband who remembers when his wife first loved him.

Then the indictment. God brought Israel into "the garden land," the promised territory, and what happened next was a betrayal on every level of society: priests who stopped asking where God was, scribes and lawyers who knew the law but had forgotten its author, shepherds — this is the word for leaders, kings and elders — who outright rebelled, and prophets who were prophesying in the name of Baal, the Canaanite storm-deity whose worship was everywhere in the culture around them. Every layer of leadership had failed.

The image that closes the passage is one of the most arresting in all of Jeremiah. God calls on the heavens themselves to be horrified at what has happened, and then delivers the double charge: Israel has abandoned "the source of living waters" and instead dug cisterns — holding tanks carved out of limestone — that are broken and cannot hold water. It is almost darkly comic if you think about it too long. Cisterns were genuinely useful things, but they held only rainwater, stagnant and still, and this image is of ones that are cracked besides. Someone has walked away from a running spring to lug water in a leaking bucket. The sheer foolishness of it is part of the point.

Psalm 36 answers this reading with precise and beautiful irony. "With you is the fountain of life, O Lord" — the very thing Jeremiah accuses Israel of abandoning. The psalm does not argue or explain; it simply sets the reality back in front of us: the mercy reaches to heaven, the stream is delightful, the light is yours when you stand in God's light.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:10-17**

Matthew 13 is the great parable chapter, and what we get today is not a parable itself but a conversation about why Jesus uses them. The disciples ask a reasonable question: why not just say plainly what you mean? The crowds are right there.

Jesus's answer has troubled readers for a long time, because it sounds almost cruel at first hearing — as if he is deliberately obscuring the truth from people so they cannot be converted. But the logic is more precise than that. He is quoting Isaiah 6, the prophet's own call narrative, in which Isaiah is sent to a people whose hearts have already closed themselves. Jesus is observing the same pattern, not engineering it. The parables are not a mechanism of exclusion; they are a form of truth-telling that can only be received by those who are willing to receive it. A story about seeds and soil lands differently depending on what kind of soil you are.

The word for "gross" in the Isaiah quotation — "gross is the heart of this people" — carries the sense of grown thick, calloused, like skin that has been rubbed so long it no longer feels. It is not a permanent condition; conversion is still explicitly named as what would happen if they would only see and hear. The door is not locked from the outside.

**The blindness that is a choice**

What Jeremiah and Matthew share is the portrait of a specifically chosen blindness. Israel in Jeremiah does not lack information; she has the law, the prophets, the priests, the memory of the Exodus. The crowds around Jesus do not lack access; they are standing in front of him. What is missing in both cases is the willingness to let what they see actually land, to let it cost them the comfortable explanations they have already arranged. That is the harder diagnosis, because it applies well past ancient Israel and first-century Galilee.

The good news in both readings is the same: the living water is still flowing, the door is still open, and the disciples — ordinary, confused, often stumbling — are told that their eyes are *blessed* because they see.

**To carry today**

Consider where in your life you might already have your explanation settled before you look. The broken cisterns in Jeremiah are not wicked things — they are just our own anxious arrangements, the strategies we trust because we made them ourselves. Ask today for the grace to look at one situation in your life with a little less certainty about what you will find, and a little more willingness to be surprised by what is actually there.

epigraph: Looking for a body, she hears her name, and everything changes.
reflection:
**The first reading — Song of Songs 3:1-4b**

The Song of Songs is the strangest book in the Bible to find at Mass. It is a love poem, erotic and restless, set in the streets of a city at night. The bride gets up from her bed and goes looking — through the streets, past the watchmen, past anyone who might help — and finds the one she loves almost by accident, almost before she can say where she found him. The poem ends in the middle of the embrace.

The Church has long read this book as something more than a wedding song: the soul in search of God, desire as a form of theology. That reading doesn't erase the poem's plainness — the woman really is looking, really is desperate, really does find — but it gives the searching a shape that fits today's feast exactly. Mary Magdalene at the tomb is the bride in the streets, except her beloved is not missing. He is present. She cannot recognize him.

**The Gospel — John 20:1-2, 11-18**

John's account of Easter morning is built around a misrecognition. Mary sees the risen Christ and thinks she is looking at the gardener. She is so fixed on finding the body she came to anoint that she cannot read what is standing in front of her. And then he says her name — one word, *Mary* — and everything reorganizes itself. She does not recognize the risen Christ by sight. She recognizes him by the way he says her name.

What happens next is often overlooked. He tells her not to hold on to him, and then sends her — *go and tell my brothers*. She came to tend a corpse and leaves as a witness to a resurrection. She is the first to carry the news of Easter, which is why she has been called, in a title the tradition takes seriously, the apostle to the apostles.

**What the two readings share**

The psalm holds both readings together: *my soul is thirsting for you, my flesh pines for you, like the earth parched and without water.* That thirst runs through the Song's bride in the streets and through Mary bent weeping into an empty tomb. Both are looking in the wrong place for the right person. The moment of finding, in both cases, comes not through their searching but through being known — recognized, named, encountered from the other side.

What the Song cannot give you, John completes: the beloved does not just appear. He speaks.

**To carry today**

What are you so sure you're looking for that you might not recognize it when it's already there?
